correctness.rationale: The published recurrence is correctly specialized to F=LJ and g=0; its two conjugate quadratics have all state multipliers. The necessary root-disc inequality follows by exact factorization from two roots. With u=(2t/c)^2 and q=2/c, its scaled strict inequality deficit is an explicit sum of two nonnegative terms; equality forces u=q=1, hence c=2,t=1. The double root and exact compatible-start trajectory, dimension-free norm and sharp transient maximum are derived algebraically and tested by exact SymPy identities and 10,429 supplementary rational/numerical cases.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The strongest located fixed-weight rate theorem attains the same numeric factor at alpha=1, c=2; it does not assert universal optimality over variable alpha. The separate variable-reflection result optimizes a split-skew worst-case stability threshold, not a two-parameter spectral radius on the unsplit J operator. The motivating paper proves generic convergence and sharp c>=3 divergence; it does not subsume this rate minimax.

originality.rationale: The 2026 source includes precisely the skew test operator and its polynomial, but only proves the c>=3 instability and a generic sufficient convergence interval, not the minimum spectral radius over two free parameters. A prior publicly indexed FRB skew result already gives the 1/sqrt(2) optimum at the fixed conventional reflection weight, which we explicitly do not claim; its fixed-weight conclusion does not imply the new universal lower bound when c varies. Other variable-reflection results address a different stability-ceiling objective. The exact universal optimizer and all-dimensional transient overshoot survive these implication comparisons, subject to unindexed historical priority risk.

value.rationale: The recently widened c-range makes whether flexible c improves skew-rotation speed a motivated algorithmic question. A universal spectral barrier over two free parameters and a unique exact optimizer are not a routine finite example. The optimally fast setting exceeds the sufficient generic step bound and provably incurs 50% initial error amplification, exposing a meaningful asymptotic-versus-finite-time algorithmic tradeoff. Scope is limited to skew-isometric linear monotone operators; no general convergence guarantee is asserted.
